title: Can You Stain Pressure Treated Wood? Yes, Once Water Soaks In
h1: Can You Stain Pressure Treated Wood?
query: can you stain pressure treated wood?
description: Yes, once it passes a 2-minute water test: if a sprinkle soaks in within several minutes instead of beading, treated wood is dry enough to take stain.
dek: Yes, once it passes a 2-minute water test: if a sprinkle soaks in within several minutes instead of beading, treated wood is dry enough to take stain.
intro: Yes, and outdoor treated lumber is better off with a finish. The real question is timing, and the wood answers that itself if you know how to ask.

Pressure-treated lumber takes stain perfectly well, and almost every treated deck, fence and pergola looks and lasts better with a finish on it. What it will not do is take stain on the day it comes home from the lumberyard. Most treated wood leaves the plant soaked with the water that carried the preservative into it, and until enough of that water leaves, any stain you apply has nowhere to go. The calendar rules you see quoted, 30 days or 60 or six months, are all attempts to guess how long that drying takes. A two-minute test on the wood itself replaces the guesswork, and the rest of this page explains how to run it, how to read it and what to do once the wood says yes.

quickAnswer: You can stain pressure-treated wood, and outdoors you generally should. The preservative in treated lumber protects it from rot fungi and termites. It does nothing against sunlight, which grays and roughens the surface, or against the repeated wetting and drying that causes cracking, checking and cupping. A stain or water-repellent finish handles those, and the combination of treatment plus finish is what gives a deck or fence a long, good-looking life.

sections.h: Can You Stain Pressure Treated Wood? at a Glance

blocks.p: The condition is that the wood must be dry enough to absorb the finish. Most standard treated lumber is sold wet, and stain applied to wet wood cannot soak in. It sits on the surface, dries slowly, and either wears away within months or, if it forms a film, peels as moisture leaves the wood underneath it. That failure is so common that many people conclude treated wood cannot be stained at all.

The fix is to let the wood tell you when it is ready rather than following a fixed number of days. Sprinkle a little water on the surface. If it beads and sits there, wait. If it darkens the wood and soaks in within several minutes, the wood is ready for stain. Everything else on this page is detail around that one test.

Two exceptions shorten the wait. Lumber labeled KDAT, for kiln-dried after treatment, has already had most of the water driven out and can often be finished soon after installation. And old, weathered treated wood that has been outside for a year or more is long since dry; it simply needs cleaning before it is stained.
THE ANSWER IN ONE LINE
Stain it when water soaks in, not when the calendar says so.

Sprinkle water on several boards. Beading means the wood is still wet from treatment; absorption within several minutes means it is ready. Test sunny and shaded boards separately, because they dry at different speeds.

sections.h: Why New Treated Lumber Refuses Stain

blocks.p: Pressure treatment is a wet process. Lumber, usually southern yellow pine or another absorbent softwood, is loaded into a sealed cylinder, and a water-based preservative solution is forced deep into the wood under pressure. Today's residential treatments are copper-based formulas such as ACQ, copper azole and micronized copper azole. The older CCA treatment, which contained arsenic, was phased out for most residential uses in the early 2000s.

Once the preservative is in, most lumber is wrapped and shipped without being dried again. Boards often arrive at the store heavy and cool to the touch, and some are visibly damp. Their cells are full of water, so there is no room for a stain to enter. A finish needs empty, open wood fibers to soak into, and saturated wood has none.

Treated pine can also have a smooth, compressed surface from the planer, sometimes called mill glaze, and occasionally a light residue from the treatment. These slow absorption further. They wear away naturally after some weeks of weather, and a cleaning and light brightening before staining removes most of what remains.

As the lumber dries outdoors, it shrinks. Deck boards installed tight together often open into gaps, and some boards cup, twist or check. That movement is another reason to let the wood settle before finishing: a stain applied before the wood has finished its first round of shrinking can crack along new checks and leave unfinished wood exposed.

None of this means the wood is defective. Wet treated lumber is normal and expected. It just means the finishing step belongs a little later in the project than most people plan for, and it is worth building that gap into your schedule from the start.

Use a spray bottle, a cup or your fingertips to put a few tablespoons of water on the face of a board. Watch for several minutes. If the water stays in beads or a puddle with sharp edges and the wood around it does not darken, the board is still too wet or too sealed to accept stain. If the water darkens the wood and disappears into it within several minutes, the board is ready.

Test more than one board. Decking in full sun dries far faster than boards in the shade of the house, and the railings and stair stringers dry at their own pace. Thick posts and beams hold water longest. Test at least five or six spots across the project, including the shadiest and the sunniest, and go by the slowest result for whatever you plan to stain that day.

Test on a dry day. Morning dew, a recent rain or a hose-down will make any wood bead or soak in unpredictably. Wait until the surface has been dry for at least a day, ideally two, and run the test in the afternoon when the boards have had sun.

A pin-type moisture meter adds a number to the answer. Push the pins into the board across the grain and read the moisture content. Many stain manufacturers ask for wood below roughly 12 to 15 percent; wet treated lumber can read well above 20 percent, and sometimes above the top of a cheap meter's range. A meter is worth its modest price if you are building a large deck.

sections.h: Reading the End Tag Before You Buy

blocks.p: Most treated lumber carries a small plastic or paper tag stapled to the end of each board, or a stamp printed on the face. It lists the preservative, the treating company, the retention level and the intended use. A few minutes reading those tags in the lumber aisle tells you a lot about how the wood will behave when it is time to finish it.

Look first for KDAT or the words kiln-dried after treatment. KDAT lumber costs more and is less common at big-box stores, but it starts close to a stainable moisture level and moves less after installation. If finishing quickly matters to you, ask the lumberyard specifically for KDAT decking and railings.

Next, look at the use category. Treated lumber is graded for above-ground use or for ground contact, often shown with codes such as UC3B for exterior above ground and UC4A or higher for ground contact. Ground-contact lumber carries more preservative and is required where wood is close to or in the soil, which includes many posts and low deck framing. Higher-retention lumber can take longer to dry, so expect posts to lag behind the decking.

The tag also names the preservative. All the common modern treatments can be stained once dry. The preservative mainly affects fastener choice, since copper-based treatments corrode plain steel. Use hot-dip galvanized or stainless fasteners and hardware rated for treated lumber, regardless of the finish you plan.

Finally, look at the boards themselves. Heavy, cold, wet-looking lumber will need a long wait. Lighter, drier boards from a covered rack will be ready sooner. If you can, store your lumber stickered, with spacers between boards, in a covered, airy spot for a while before building; it will dry faster than in a tight bundle.

sections.h: How Long the Wait Usually Runs

blocks.p: There is no fixed number of days, but there are realistic ranges. In hot, dry climates with strong sun, standard treated decking can pass the water test within a few weeks. In mild climates with average humidity, one to three months is typical. In humid, rainy or shaded locations, or for lumber installed in fall, it can take three months or more, and sometimes a full winter.

Board size changes the timeline. Thin decking and railing pickets dry fastest. Two-by framing dries more slowly, and four-by and six-by posts can stay wet at the core for many months, though their surfaces may pass the test sooner. Stain what is ready and come back for the rest.

Season matters as much as climate. A deck built in early summer may be ready by late summer. One built in October may not be ready until the following spring, and that is fine: unfinished treated wood will not rot over a single winter. Waiting is far better than staining wet wood in cold weather.

Do not wait indefinitely, though. After a year or so of full exposure, untreated surfaces gray and roughen, and the wood needs more cleaning and brightening before it will look good under stain. The ideal window is soon after the wood first passes the test, during a stretch of mild, dry weather.

**Brand-new deck or fence, standard lumber.** Build it, let it dry, test it, then clean and stain. Plan the project with a gap of at least several weeks between construction and finishing. If you are building a fence, our [fence stain guide](/best-fence-stain/) covers products that spray easily over long runs once the pickets are ready.

**KDAT lumber.** Test it as soon as it is installed. It often passes within days. If it beads, rain or storage may have rewetted it; wait a little and test again. Clean off dust and pencil marks before staining.

**Weathered treated wood, never finished.** It is dry, but the surface has grayed and roughened. Clean it with an oxygen-based deck cleaner, rinse at low pressure, brighten with an oxalic acid product and let it dry for a day or two. Then stain. Lightly sand fuzzy areas first.

**Treated wood with an old stain.** If water soaks in, the old penetrating stain is worn enough to recoat after cleaning. If an old film is peeling, strip it before applying anything. If an old solid stain is sound, recoat with a compatible solid stain.

**Mixed old and new boards.** Repairs often put fresh, wet boards beside dry, weathered ones. Stain the old boards now if they need it, and do the new ones when they pass the test. A semi-transparent or solid stain helps blend the colors. Expect new boards to look different for a season.

**Ground-contact posts and framing.** These are often not stained at all, and they do not need to be for structural reasons. Do treat every field cut with a brush-on end-cut preservative, usually a copper naphthenate product, because cutting exposes untreated wood at the core. Industry treating standards call for it.

sections.h: Choosing a Stain for Treated Pine

blocks.p: Treated southern pine is not a showpiece wood. Fresh lumber often has a green or brown cast from the preservative, along with knots, color variation and the occasional incising marks. Most owners are happiest with a stain that adds color and hides some of that variation, rather than a pure clear that leaves it visible.

**Semi-transparent penetrating stains** are the best default. They soak in, show the grain, add enough pigment to block UV and even out color, and fade rather than peel. They are also the most forgiving if the wood is slightly less dry than ideal, since there is no film to lift. Our [guide to deck stains for pressure-treated wood](/best-deck-stain-for-pressure-treated-wood/) ranks specific products for this lumber.

**Solid stains** hide the grain and the green cast entirely and give a uniform color. They are more sensitive to moisture because they form a film, so the wood must be fully ready. Use them on older treated wood with mismatched boards, or when matching house trim. For decks that are past saving with stain, our [deck paint guide](/best-deck-paint/) covers coatings by deck condition.

**Clear sealers** keep water out but let the wood gray, so they are a short-term choice on treated pine. They are useful as a first-season water repellent on a deck you plan to stain with color later, as long as you choose one that does not block a later stain. Our [deck sealant guide](/best-deck-sealant/) explains the tradeoffs.

Oil or water base is a secondary choice. Oil-based penetrating stains tend to soak deeper and fade more gradually; water-based stains dry faster, clean up with soap and are legal everywhere. Either works on treated lumber once it is dry. Choose by your climate, your state's VOC rules and how forgiving you need the product to be.

sections.h: Once It Passes: The Staining Steps

blocks.p: Clean the wood even if it is new. Construction leaves dust, footprints, pencil marks and sometimes a light residue from treatment. A deck cleaner or mild detergent, scrubbed with a stiff brush and rinsed thoroughly, gives the stain a clean surface. Avoid high pressure; a garden hose is often enough on new lumber.

Brighten if the wood looks blotchy or dull. An oxalic acid brightener evens out color, neutralizes cleaners and removes iron stains. Rinse well. Then let the wood dry again for at least a day or two and repeat the water test, since cleaning puts water back in.

Try the stain on a test area, such as the back of a stair tread or an offcut from the same lumber. Let it dry fully and check the color in daylight. Treated pine takes color unevenly at first, and a test avoids surprises across a whole deck.

Stain on a mild, dry day out of direct midday sun, with no rain forecast for at least a day. Work two or three boards at a time along their full length. Back-brush to work stain into the grain and pick up puddles. Wipe off anything the wood does not absorb within the label's wait time.

Apply only the number of coats the label calls for. Extra stain on new treated wood does not add protection; it sits on top and turns sticky or peels. For drying and recoat timing in different weather, see our guide to [deck stain drying time](/deck-stain-drying-time/).

sections.h: If You Already Stained Too Soon

blocks.p: The signs show up within weeks or months: a tacky surface that collects dirt, blotchy color, a finish that wears off the boards almost immediately, or with solid stains, peeling and blistering. Do not apply another coat over the top. More stain over a failed coat makes the problem worse.

With a penetrating semi-transparent stain, the simplest fix is often time. Let the wood finish drying through a season, then clean with a deck cleaner, brighten and apply a fresh coat once water soaks in. Much of the original stain will have faded or washed off, and the new coat will bond properly.

If the surface is sticky, wipe it down with the solvent the label recommends, or use a deck cleaner and stiff brush to remove excess. Unabsorbed stain that has not cured can often be scrubbed off; stain that has cured into a tacky film may need a deck stain stripper.

With solid stain or paint that is peeling, the loose film has to come off. Scrape and strip the failed areas, brighten, let the wood dry thoroughly and test before recoating. Peeling over wet wood usually continues to spread, so treat the whole surface rather than patching.
Learn from the timeline. Note how long it took the wood to pass the water test, and use that for any future additions or repairs. Many owners who stain too soon once never do it again.

Modern residential treated lumber is considered appropriate for decks, fences and similar outdoor uses, but basic precautions still apply. Wear gloves when handling it, especially wet lumber, and wash your hands before eating or drinking. Wash work clothes separately from other laundry.

Wear a dust mask and eye protection when cutting or sanding, and cut outdoors where possible. Sweep up and dispose of sawdust and offcuts with regular trash, according to local rules. Do not use treated sawdust as mulch or compost.

Never burn treated wood in a fireplace, wood stove, fire pit or open fire. Burning releases preservative chemicals into the smoke and concentrates them in the ash. Dispose of scraps through normal trash or your local waste guidance instead.

For food gardens, many people line the inside of treated raised beds with plastic sheeting or choose naturally rot-resistant wood instead. Check current guidance from your local extension service if you plan to grow food near treated lumber.

When staining, follow the stain label's safety instructions as well. Oil-based stains are flammable, and rags soaked with drying oils can heat and ignite as they cure. Lay them flat outdoors to dry or seal them in a metal container filled with water before disposal.

mistakes: Rules like wait 30 days or wait six months ignore climate, season and lumber type. A deck in Arizona may be ready in weeks, while one in a shaded, humid backyard may need several months. Use the water test on several boards, and stain only when water soaks in within a few minutes.

Boards in full sun dry fastest and pass the test first, while shaded boards, stair stringers and posts can stay wet much longer. Testing one easy spot leads to staining wood that is not ready. Test the shadiest and thickest parts of the project and go by the slowest result.
Skipping the cleaning on new wood

New lumber carries dust, pencil marks, footprints and sometimes treatment residue. Stain applied over that film absorbs unevenly and may not bond well. Clean with a deck cleaner or mild detergent, rinse well, let the wood dry again and confirm with another water test before staining.
Using a solid stain on barely dry wood

Solid stains and paints form a film that traps any moisture left in the wood, so they peel if the boards are not fully dry. If you are unsure, use a semi-transparent penetrating stain for the first coat, or wait longer and use a moisture meter before applying a solid color.

Every field cut exposes untreated wood at the core of a treated board. Without an end-cut preservative, those cuts are where decay starts, especially on posts and joists. Brush a copper naphthenate end-cut solution on every cut during construction, then stain the visible surfaces when the wood is ready.
bottomLine: Treated lumber is worth staining, as long as you wait until it has dried enough to absorb the finish. Skip the calendar rules, sprinkle water on several boards, and stain when it soaks in. KDAT lumber is often ready within days; standard lumber may need weeks or months depending on climate and season. When the wood is ready, clean it, brighten if needed, test the color and apply a semi-transparent penetrating stain in thin coats. Treat every cut end during construction, handle the lumber with basic precautions and never burn the scraps. For product picks, see our [deck stain rankings](/best-deck-stain-reviews/).

faqs.q: How do I know pressure-treated wood is dry enough to stain?
faqs.a: Sprinkle a few tablespoons of water on several boards on a dry day. If it beads and sits on the surface, the wood is still too wet. If it darkens the wood and soaks in within several minutes, it is ready. A pin moisture meter reading in the low to mid teens confirms it. Test sunny and shaded boards separately.

faqs.q: What does KDAT mean on treated lumber?
faqs.a: KDAT stands for kiln-dried after treatment. The lumber was dried in a kiln after the preservative was applied, so it starts much drier than standard treated wood. It moves less after installation and can often be stained within days or a couple of weeks. It costs more and is less common at big-box stores, so ask your lumberyard.

faqs.q: Can I paint pressure-treated wood instead of staining it?
faqs.a: Yes, once it is fully dry, cleaned and primed with an exterior primer suitable for treated lumber. Paint forms a film, so it is more sensitive to leftover moisture than a penetrating stain and will peel if applied too soon. On decks, paint and solid stain also need more maintenance. Many owners prefer semi-transparent stain on treated decks.

faqs.q: Is it bad to never stain pressure-treated wood?
faqs.a: The treatment protects against rot and insects, so unfinished treated wood will not decay quickly. Without a finish, though, it will gray, crack, check and cup more as it weathers, and splinters become more common. A stain or water repellent slows that damage and keeps the wood looking better. It is optional for structure but worthwhile for appearance and comfort.

faqs.q: Can I stain treated wood in winter?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most stains need air and surface temperatures above roughly 40 to 50 degrees during application and drying, and treated wood dries very slowly in cold, damp weather. It is better to let new treated lumber sit unfinished through winter and stain it in spring once it passes the water test. A single winter unfinished does no real harm.

faqs.q: Do I need to sand pressure-treated wood before staining?
faqs.a: Usually not on new lumber. Cleaning and, if needed, brightening are enough. Sand lightly with roughly 60 to 80 grit only if the surface is very smooth and resists absorption or if weathering has raised fuzz. Avoid fine grits, which close the surface. Wear a dust mask when sanding treated wood and clean up the dust.

faqs.q: Will stain hide the green color of treated wood?
faqs.a: Semi-transparent stains with a warm brown or cedar tone hide most of the green cast, especially as the preservative color fades over the first months. Solid stains hide it completely. Clear sealers and very light transparent stains will not hide it. Test the color on an offcut first, since treated pine takes stain unevenly at the start.
